title: Genesis 49. The Cup of Twelve.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 49. The Cup of Twelve.
Jacob called to his sons and said: Gather yourselves together,
that I may tell you that which will happen to you in the days to come.
Assemble yourselves, and hear, you sons of Jacob.
Listen to Israel, your father.
Gather.
the same root as gathered to his people at the end of the chapter.
Jacob gathers his sons to tell them what will be.
Then he will be gathered himself.
The old man who could not see now sees the future.
The Cup that has tracked through forty-eight chapters now distributes.
One Cup becomes twelve.
Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might,
and the beginning of my strength,
excelling in dignity and excelling in power.
Boiling over like water, you shall not excel,
because you went up to your father's bed, then defiled it.
Reuben.
The firstborn falls.
The fourth firstborn in Genesis to lose the position.
Ishmael passed over for Isaac.
Esau passed over for Jacob.
Reuben loses preeminence.
The pattern of the firstborn failing is itself a pattern in Genesis.
The covenant does not travel through strength or birth order.
It travels through God's choice,
and through the character that emerges in the Cup's journey.
Reuben tried to save Joseph.
Offered his sons as a guarantee.
But the Bilhah incident defines his legacy.
Unstable as water.
The Cup of the firstborn was already drained.
Simeon and Levi are brothers.
Their swords are weapons of violence.
My soul, don't come into their council.
My glory, don't be united to their assembly,
for in their anger they killed men.
In their self-will they hamstrung cattle.
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce.
And their wrath, for it was cruel.
I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.
The Shechem slaughter.
Twenty years later, the father remembers.
The violence that Jacob said nothing about at the time now comes with its consequence.
Simeon was kept in prison.
Levi will receive no land, priestly cities only.
Simeon will be absorbed into Judah's territory.
Scattered.
Divided.
The Cup of violence distributed as dispersion.
The father who was silent at Shechem now speaks.
The silence that created space for violence now produces the word that scatters the violent.
Judah, your brothers will praise you.
Your hand will be on the neck of your enemies.
Your father's sons will bow down before you.
Judah is a lion's cub.
From the prey, my son, you have gone up.
He stooped down, he crouched as a lion, as a lioness.
Who will rouse him up?
The scepter shall not depart from Judah,
nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes.
And to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.
Judah.
The one who said sell him.
Who confessed she is more righteous than I.
Who said I will bear the blame forever.
Who offered himself as a substitute:
Let me remain instead of the boy.
Who led the family into Egypt.
Judah receives the scepter.
The betrayer who became the substitute now receives the kingship.
The covenant's political dimension, the ruler, the scepter,
the obedience of the peoples,
passes through the one who sold his brother and then offered to take a brother's place.
The Cup of the scandal and the Cup of decision pour into the Cup of the scepter.
The betrayer's arc,
from sell him to confess to guarantee to substitute to guide,
completes in a word that points beyond itself: until Shiloh comes.
The scepter belongs to Judah, until.
The covenant's kingship is not permanent in Judah's hand.
It waits for someone.
Shiloh.
The one to whom it belongs.
The one whose coming will gather the obedience of the peoples.
The Cup of the scepter points forward, beyond Judah, beyond David,
beyond Solomon.
The lion who sojourns.
The king who has not arrived yet.
The scepter that waits.
Binding his foal to the vine,
his donkey's colt to the choice vine,
he has washed his garments in wine,
his robes in the blood of grapes.
His eyes will be red with wine, his teeth white with milk.
Wine.
Blood of grapes.
The Cup that has been the image of the Joseph story,
the cup-bearer's cup, the silver cup, the cup of testing,
now appears as wine in Judah's blessing.
The scepter holder washes in wine.
The one who will hold the covenant's kingship is associated with the vine and the blood of grapes.
The Cup of the covenant becomes the Cup of the king.
Zebulun will dwell at the haven of the sea.
He will be for a haven of ships.
His border will be on Sidon.
Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the saddlebags.
He saw a resting place, that it was good, the land,
that it was pleasant.
He bows his shoulder to the burden,
and becomes a servant doing forced labor.
Dan will judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel.
Dan will be a serpent on the trail,
an adder in the path, that bites the horse's heels,
so that his rider falls backward.
And then Jacob breaks: I have waited for your salvation, Yahweh.
For your salvation I wait, O Lord.
Jacob interrupts his own prophecy with a cry for salvation.
The serpent on the path provokes the prayer for deliverance.
The Cup of twelve holds both the serpent and the cry.
The father who sees the future of his sons, the violence,
the scattering, the serpents, breaks into prayer.
Not for one son.
For salvation itself.
The Cup that has been held by a man who said few and evil have been my days now reaches toward the only thing that can answer what is coming:
God's salvation.
A troop will press on Gad,
but he will press on their heel.
Asher's food will be rich.
He will produce royal dainties.
Naphtali is a doe set free, who bears beautiful fawns.
Joseph is a fruitful vine, a fruitful vine by a spring.
His branches run over the wall.
The archers have severely grieved him, shot at him, and persecuted him.
But his bow remained strong.
The arms of his hands were made strong,
by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob,
from there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel,
even by the God of your father, who will help you,
by the Almighty, who will bless you, with blessings of heaven above,
blessings of the deep that lies below, blessings of the breasts,
and of the womb.
Joseph's blessing is the longest and the richest.
The Cup that went down receives the fullest Cup.
The one who was shot at by archers, his own brothers,
now receives blessings from heaven above and deep beneath.
The archers bitterly attacked him.
The same brothers who are standing around the deathbed.
The same brothers who stripped his coat.
The same brothers who sold him for twenty shekels.
They are the archers.
And his bow remained strong.
Not because he was strong.
Because the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob held his arms.
From there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel.
the Shepherd, the Stone.
The same God Jacob called my shepherd in chapter forty-eight is named as the source of Joseph's strength.
The Cup of the shepherd: God shepherded Jacob,
and the same Shepherd strengthened Joseph.
The Stone.
The first time God is called a stone in Genesis.
The pillow at Bethel, the stone Jacob poured oil on,
becomes a name for God Himself.
The stone that was a pillow becomes the Stone that holds the covenant.
Blessings of the breasts and of the womb.
The covenant of fruitfulness, be fruitful and multiply, flows through Joseph's blessing.
The Cup of creation returns in the Cup of Joseph.
Fruitfulness.
Multiplication.
The first command and the last blessing are the same Cup.
The blessings of your father have prevailed above the blessings of my ancestors,
above the boundaries of the ancient hills.
They will be on the head of Joseph,
on the crown of the head of him who is separated from his brothers..prince,
or separated one.
Joseph, the one who was separated from his brothers, is crowned,
The Cup of separation becomes the crown of the separated one.
The brother who was taken from his father's house,
stripped of his coat, separated from everything he loved,
is now called the prince among his brothers.
The separation that was imposed by violence is now named as the mark of God's choice.
Benjamin is a ravenous wolf.
In the morning he will devour the prey.
At evening he will divide the plunder.
All these are the twelve tribes of Israel,
and this is what their father spoke to them, and blessed them.
He blessed everyone according to his own blessing.
All these are the twelve tribes.
The Cup has been distributed.
One Cup, tracked through creation, the fall, the flood, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob,
Judah, Joseph, now becomes twelve.
Each son receives a portion.
Some blessed.
Some cursed.
Some scattered.
Some crowned.
But all held.
The Book of Witness holds twelve Cups,
because the covenant is no longer one man's journey.
It is a people.
He instructed them and said:
I am to be gathered to my people.
Bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
in the cave that is in the field of Machpelah,
which is before Mamre, in the land of Canaan,
which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place.
There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife.
There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife.
And there I buried Leah.
Leah.
The unloved wife.
The one whose eyes were weak.
The one who said now my husband will be joined to me,
and this time I will praise the Lord.
She is in the family tomb.
Rachel is on the road.
Leah got the tomb.
Rachel got the roadside.
But Jacob's last words before death include Leah, buried with the patriarchs.
The unloved wife lies with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
The Cup that was held by favoritism,
Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah,
now ends by naming Leah in the family tomb.
The unloved one is honored in death.
The one who was second in life is first in burial.
When Jacob finished charging his sons,
he gathered up his feet into the bed, breathed his last breath,
and was gathered to his people.
He was gathered to his people.
He gathered up his feet into the bed.
He breathed his last.
Not: he died.
He was gathered.
The sojourner who never arrived, who called his life few and evil,
who said his days were a sojourning, is gathered.
The Cup of sojourning ends in gathering.
The man who gathered his sons to tell them what would be is himself gathered.
The feet that fled from Esau, that limped from Peniel,
that walked to Beersheba and rode to Egypt, gather.
The Cup holds.
The sojourner rests.
Joseph's hand will be on his eyes.
God promised it in chapter forty-six.
Joseph will close his father's eyes.
The son who was thought dead will attend the father's death.
The Cup of grief, twenty-two years of mourning over a blood-stained coat,
is answered by a son's hand on a father's eyes.
The false death answered by a real death.
The false grief answered by a real presence.
The Cup that was emptied by a lie is now filled by the truth.
The Cup of twelve stands.
Twelve portions poured.
Reuben unstable.
Simeon and Levi scattered.
Judah crowned.
Joseph fruitful.
Benjamin ravenous.
Zebulun at the sea.
Issachar under burden.
Dan a serpent.
Gad raided.
Asher rich.
Naphtali free.
All twelve.
All held.
All spoken over by a dying man who could not see with his eyes but saw with prophecy.
The scepter waits for Shiloh.
The serpent waits for salvation.
The sojourner waits for gathering.
And the Cup,
the one Cup that has held everything from Eden to Egypt,
from the garden to the grave, now rests in twelve vessels.
In twelve tribes.
In a people who will carry it through four hundred years of bondage,
through a sea that parts, through a wilderness that tests,
through a land that is given and taken and lost and given again.
The Cup holds.
The father is gathered.
The sons remain.
And the scepter, the Cup of the king, waits.
Until Shiloh comes.
